--- title: "Modern Data Mart Consumption: APIs and Semantic Layers" subtitle: "From Direct Queries to Service Contracts" author: "Diego Villalba" date: today format: html bibliography: [referencias_api_consumo.bib, ../../../references.bib] jupyter: python3 --- ```{=html} ``` The previous chapter concluded with the construction of a physical Sales data mart comprising four core tables: `dim_tiempo`, `dim_ubicacion`, `dim_departamento`, and `fact_ventas`. While querying this dimensional schema directly via SQL or BI tools connected through ODBC/JDBC remains common, it is not the only—nor always the most effective—consumption pattern. Mobile applications, embedded customer dashboards, microservices, and autonomous software agents should not require direct database credentials or internal schema knowledge to retrieve sales metrics. This chapter formalizes exposing data marts through a **service contract**—an API layer—rather than direct database access. ## From Direct Access to Service Contracts In traditional consumption models, every client application connects directly to the data warehouse and executes custom SQL queries. While simple initially, this tightly couples client applications to internal physical schemas: renaming a column in `dim_ubicacion` breaks every downstream client. Furthermore, enforcing centralized access control, rate limiting, and schema versioning becomes difficult. ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} **Definition.** A **data service contract** decouples the physical storage representation $DM_j$ from client-facing interfaces via an access function $A$ that exposes only authorized operations and attributes: $$ A: \text{Request} \longrightarrow \text{Response}, \qquad A \text{ encapsulates the internal schema of } DM_j $$ ::: ```{=html}
Sales Data Mart
fact_ventas + conformed dimensions.
→
Semantic Layer + API
Defines metrics once; exposes them via REST / GraphQL.
→
Clients
Mobile App · Embedded Dashboard · Microservice · Analytics Notebook
Architectural flow. Clients consume a unified service contract without needing direct database access or internal schema awareness.
``` This separation between storage and consumption extends classic data independence principles to the API layer [@kimball2013]. ## REST APIs over Data Marts REST (*Representational State Transfer*) maps operational resources and analytical queries to stateless HTTP endpoints [@fielding2000rest]. For a data mart, a natural REST resource is an aggregated metric query (e.g., "sales by region and quarter"). ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} **Definition.** A REST endpoint over a data mart maps filter parameters and dimension groupings to a structured payload (typically JSON): $$ \text{GET } /\text{sales}?\text{region}=r\,\&\,\text{quarter}=t \;\longmapsto\; \big\{\text{department}: v \;\big|\; v = C(r,t,\cdot)\big\} $$ ::: The Richardson Maturity Model categorizes REST API maturity from Level 0 (single RPC endpoint) to Level 3 (HATEOAS hypermedia controls) [@fowler2010richardson]. Most enterprise analytical APIs operate at Level 2, leveraging HTTP verbs and status codes alongside query parameter filtering. ### Endpoint Interface Design A Level 2 REST endpoint interface for the Sales data mart: ```python # app.py — illustrative interface using FastAPI from fastapi import FastAPI, Query app = FastAPI(title="Sales Analytics API") @app.get("/v1/sales") def get_sales( region: str | None = Query(None), quarter: str | None = Query(None), department: str | None = Query(None), ): """Returns aggregated sales filtered by region, quarter, and/or department.""" result = query_metric( "total_sales", group_by=["region", "quarter", "department"], filters={"region": region, "quarter": quarter, "department": department}, ) return {"data": result} ``` The key architectural pattern here is separation of concerns: the HTTP endpoint delegates metric calculation to `query_metric`, an underlying semantic layer function that abstracts SQL join execution [@fastapi2024docs]. ### Reproducible Request/Response Simulation We simulate this request/response cycle using Python and `pandas`: ::: {#2001a7c4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd dim_tiempo = pd.DataFrame({ "time_key": [1, 2], "quarter": ["Q1", "Q2"], "year": [2025, 2025], }) dim_ubicacion = pd.DataFrame({ "location_key": [1, 2, 3, 4], "city": ["CDMX", "Guadalajara", "Monterrey", "Merida"], "region": ["Central", "West", "North", "Southeast"], }) dim_departamento = pd.DataFrame({ "dept_key": [1, 2, 3, 4], "department": ["Wood", "Plumbing", "Decoration", "Electrical"], }) fact_ventas = pd.DataFrame([ (1, 1, 1, 70), (1, 1, 2, 40), (1, 1, 3, 20), (1, 1, 4, 30), (2, 1, 1, 50), (2, 1, 2, 60), (2, 1, 3, 22), (2, 1, 4, 28), (1, 2, 1, 60), (1, 2, 2, 35), (1, 2, 3, 25), (1, 2, 4, 40), (2, 2, 1, 45), (2, 2, 2, 50), (2, 2, 3, 30), (2, 2, 4, 35), (1, 3, 1, 48), (1, 3, 2, 38), (1, 3, 3, 18), (1, 3, 4, 26), (2, 3, 1, 36), (2, 3, 2, 55), (2, 3, 3, 25), (2, 3, 4, 30), (1, 4, 1, 52), (1, 4, 2, 42), (1, 4, 3, 15), (1, 4, 4, 37), (2, 4, 1, 44), (2, 4, 2, 33), (2, 4, 3, 20), (2, 4, 4, 28), ], columns=["time_key", "location_key", "dept_key", "sales_amount"]) data_mart = ( fact_ventas .merge(dim_tiempo, on="time_key") .merge(dim_ubicacion, on="location_key") .merge(dim_departamento, on="dept_key") ) data_mart.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
time_key location_key dept_key sales_amount quarter year city region department
0 1 1 1 70 Q1 2025 CDMX Central Wood
1 1 1 2 40 Q1 2025 CDMX Central Plumbing
2 1 1 3 20 Q1 2025 CDMX Central Decoration
3 1 1 4 30 Q1 2025 CDMX Central Electrical
4 2 1 1 50 Q2 2025 CDMX Central Wood
``` ::: ::: Implementing the endpoint request handler: ::: {#daabc449 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def get_sales_endpoint(region=None, quarter=None, department=None): df = data_mart if region: df = df[df["region"] == region] if quarter: df = df[df["quarter"] == quarter] if department: df = df[df["department"] == department] aggregated = ( df.groupby(["region", "quarter", "department"], as_index=False)["sales_amount"] .sum() .rename(columns={"sales_amount": "total_sales"}) ) return {"data": aggregated.to_dict(orient="records")} request_params = {"region": "Central", "quarter": "Q2"} response_payload = get_sales_endpoint(**request_params) response_payload ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {'data': [{'region': 'Central', 'quarter': 'Q2', 'department': 'Decoration', 'total_sales': 22}, {'region': 'Central', 'quarter': 'Q2', 'department': 'Electrical', 'total_sales': 28}, {'region': 'Central', 'quarter': 'Q2', 'department': 'Plumbing', 'total_sales': 60}, {'region': 'Central', 'quarter': 'Q2', 'department': 'Wood', 'total_sales': 50}]} ``` ::: ::: ## GraphQL APIs over Data Marts GraphQL empowers client applications to request specific fields and structure responses dynamically in a single request, resolving REST over-fetching (retrieving unneeded attributes) and under-fetching (requiring multiple round-trips) [@graphql2021spec]. ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} **Definition.** A GraphQL query specifies a subset of fields $F \subseteq \text{fields}(R)$ on resource $R$; the server resolver returns strictly $F$. ::: Illustrative GraphQL schema definition: ```python # schema.py — illustrative Strawberry GraphQL definition import strawberry @strawberry.type class AggregatedSale: region: str quarter: str department: str total_sales: float @strawberry.type class Query: @strawberry.field def sales(self, region: str | None = None, quarter: str | None = None) -> list[AggregatedSale]: result = query_metric( "total_sales", group_by=["region", "quarter", "department"], filters={"region": region, "quarter": quarter}, ) return [AggregatedSale(**row) for row in result] schema = strawberry.Schema(query=Query) ``` Client GraphQL query requesting only department and total_sales: ```graphql query { sales(region: "Central", quarter: "Q2") { department totalSales } } ``` ### Reproducible Simulation of GraphQL Field Selection ::: {#a9bf38e6 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def resolve_sales_query(requested_fields, region=None, quarter=None, department=None): df = data_mart if region: df = df[df["region"] == region] if quarter: df = df[df["quarter"] == quarter] if department: df = df[df["department"] == department] aggregated = ( df.groupby(["region", "quarter", "department"], as_index=False)["sales_amount"] .sum() .rename(columns={"sales_amount": "total_sales"}) ) return aggregated[requested_fields].to_dict(orient="records") resolve_sales_query(["department", "total_sales"], region="Central", quarter="Q2") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [{'department': 'Decoration', 'total_sales': 22}, {'department': 'Electrical', 'total_sales': 28}, {'department': 'Plumbing', 'total_sales': 60}, {'department': 'Wood', 'total_sales': 50}] ``` ::: ::: ## Semantic Layers: Metrics as Code Both REST and GraphQL patterns rely on an underlying **semantic layer**. A semantic layer defines business metrics (calculation rules, aggregations, filters) **once as code**, serving as a single source of truth across dashboards, REST endpoints, GraphQL queries, and notebooks [@dbtlabs2024semanticlayer; @cubejs2024docs]. ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} **Definition.** A **semantic metric** is a registered function $M: (\text{groupings}, \text{filters}) \to \mathbb{R}$ executed over the underlying data mart: $$ M_{\text{total\_sales}}(G, F) = \sum_{i \,:\, i \models F} \text{sales\_amount}_i \quad \text{grouped by } G $$ ::: Decoupling metric definitions from visualization tools is commonly referred to as **headless BI**. ### Reproducible Semantic Metric Registry ::: {#3bc5294d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} METRICS_REGISTRY = { "total_sales": { "column": "sales_amount", "aggregation": "sum", }, "average_ticket": { "column": "sales_amount", "aggregation": "mean", }, } def query_metric(metric_name, group_by, filters=None): if metric_name not in METRICS_REGISTRY: raise ValueError(f"Unregistered metric: {metric_name}") definition = METRICS_REGISTRY[metric_name] df = data_mart for field, value in (filters or {}).items(): if value is not None: df = df[df[field] == value] aggregated = ( df.groupby(group_by, as_index=False)[definition["column"]] .agg(definition["aggregation"]) .rename(columns={definition["column"]: metric_name}) ) return aggregated.to_dict(orient="records") query_metric( "total_sales", group_by=["region", "quarter"], filters={"quarter": "Q2"}, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [{'region': 'Central', 'quarter': 'Q2', 'total_sales': 160}, {'region': 'North', 'quarter': 'Q2', 'total_sales': 146}, {'region': 'Southeast', 'quarter': 'Q2', 'total_sales': 125}, {'region': 'West', 'quarter': 'Q2', 'total_sales': 160}] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#80e6a8ba .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} query_metric( "average_ticket", group_by=["department"], filters={"region": "Central"}, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` [{'department': 'Decoration', 'average_ticket': 21.0}, {'department': 'Electrical', 'average_ticket': 29.0}, {'department': 'Plumbing', 'average_ticket': 50.0}, {'department': 'Wood', 'average_ticket': 60.0}] ``` ::: ::: ## Comparing Consumption Contracts ```{=html}
Central Region Sales in Q2 by Department — Three Contracts
Server dictates response shape: includes all resource fields by default.
Request
GET /v1/sales?region=Central&quarter=Q2
Response
{
  "data": [
    {"region": "Central", "quarter": "Q2", "department": "Televisions", "total_sales": 45},
    {"region": "Central", "quarter": "Q2", "department": "Computers",   "total_sales": 50},
    {"region": "Central", "quarter": "Q2", "department": "Decoration",  "total_sales": 30},
    {"region": "Central", "quarter": "Q2", "department": "Electrical",  "total_sales": 35}
  ]
}
Client dictates response shape: requests only department and total_sales.
Request
query {
  sales(region: "Central", quarter: "Q2") {
    department
    totalSales
  }
}
Response
{
  "data": {
    "sales": [
      {"department": "Televisions", "totalSales": 45},
      {"department": "Computers",   "totalSales": 50},
      {"department": "Decoration",  "totalSales": 30},
      {"department": "Electrical",  "totalSales": 35}
    ]
  }
}
Both API protocols delegate metric evaluation to the centralized semantic layer.
Invocation
query_metric(
    "total_sales",
    group_by=["department"],
    filters={"region": "Central", "quarter": "Q2"},
)
Result
[
  {"department": "Televisions", "total_sales": 45},
  {"department": "Computers",   "total_sales": 50},
  {"department": "Decoration",  "total_sales": 30},
  {"department": "Electrical",  "total_sales": 35}
]
All three contracts expose identical metric calculations (45, 50, 30, 35); only protocol interaction format varies.
``` ## Security and Governance at the API Layer Centralizing data mart access through an API layer enables security controls that are difficult to enforce with direct database queries: - **Authentication & Authorization:** Verifies caller identities and scope permissions (JWT, API keys). - **Row-Level Security (RLS):** Automatically restricts data visibility based on user roles (e.g., regional managers see only their assigned regions). - **Rate Limiting & Throttling:** Protects analytical databases from unoptimized, expensive queries. - **Contract Versioning:** Explicit URL paths (e.g., `/v1/`) support schema evolution without breaking legacy client integrations. ## Conclusions Exposing data marts via APIs and semantic layers transforms database tables into governed **data products** [@dehghani2022datamesh]. Whether providing interactive OLAP cube exploration or programmatic REST/GraphQL service endpoints, defining conformed dimensions and metrics once guarantees enterprise-wide consistency across all analytics consumers. ## References ::: {#refs} :::
